column3: The angels' complete prostration forms the immediate backdrop to Iblis's refusal and later fully gathered forces.
Its total ransom cannot avert punishment, reinforcing that amassed resources or support cannot rescue the condemned.
The report of armies supplies a broad frame for organized force whose apparent power is subject to divine judgment.
The angels' complete prostration, immediately followed by Iblis's exception, contrasts united obedience with his later army.
The command to assemble gatherers begins the local pattern of mobilizing a collective force for confrontation.
God's unseen troops contrast with Iblis's assembled troops by locating decisive aid outside visible military numbers.
Iblis's refusal to join the prostrators identifies the foundational rupture behind the forces attributed to him.
The garden's drawing near for the righteous frames the final division in which Iblis's troops are gathered for the opposite end.
The joining of sun and moon shares the language of gathering but does not develop Iblis, troops, or judgmental allegiance.
It names Iblis's pride and disbelief, the moral source of the following declaration about the totality of his followers.
The misguided are cast into Hell immediately before the explicit gathering of Iblis's troops there.
All people are gathered for a witnessed day, providing a wider judgment setting for the assembled forces in Hell.
Moses and all with him are saved together, an opposed collective outcome to Iblis's forces gathered for punishment.
God's declaration of truth introduces the ensuing sentence that Hell will be filled with Iblis and all who follow him.
Divine troops accompany tranquility and increased faith, offering only a general contrast with Iblis's forces.
Iblis alone refuses the commanded prostration, directly grounding his later distinct collective.
The magicians are gathered at an appointed time, a local instance of organized assembly preceding a decisive contest.
The total forces of heaven and earth belong to God, contrasting divine sovereignty with Iblis's contingent troops.
Iblis's expectation is realized when people follow him, directly connecting his leadership with a collective body of followers.
Hell is displayed for the misguided immediately before they and Iblis's troops are thrown into it.
God's troops are promised victory, providing a clear counterpoint to Iblis's gathered but helpless forces.
Hell is the appointed place for all who follow Satan, closely matching the complete gathering of Iblis's troops for punishment.
The pursued servants and their pursuers set up the collective military movement that ends in the enemy army's drowning.
All generations are gathered at an appointed day, expanding the eschatological gathering underlying 26:95.
Iblis refuses, acts arrogantly, and becomes among the disbelievers, directly defining the rebellion behind his forces.
The public call to assemble shows the local narrative's deliberate formation of a crowd for confrontation.
Universal disbelief shows totality of response but has no specific relation to Iblis's army or the final scene.
A troop is described as defeated, supporting the theme that organized hostile force does not guarantee deliverance.
The condemned wish for a return to become believers, continuing the Hell scene that contains Iblis's gathered troops.
The account tests and confronts armies while showing that numerical force is not the decisive measure of victory.
Divine collection is thematically adjacent to total gathering but does not specify agents, followers, or punishment.
The pursuing army enters the sea as a body and is drowned, a close narrative counterpart to troops gathered for ruin.
Pharaoh follows with his troops and the sea overwhelms them, displaying the collapse of an organized persecuting force.
Supposed gods cannot aid their worshippers even when those worshippers stand as troops ready for them, directly echoing powerless false support.
Pharaoh sends gatherers through the cities, a direct local example of mobilizing a collective hostile force.
All are gathered and false worship relations are interrogated, closely paralleling the exposure of Iblis's gathered support.
The verse denies any need for a heavenly army in punishment, only broadly contrasting visible force with divine action.
Abraham's opening question about what his people worship begins the idolatry argument whose final scene includes Iblis's troops.
Pharaoh's claim that his people are a united, cautious body exposes the false security of a fully mobilized regime.
The listing of earlier peoples does not materially clarify Iblis, troops, gathering, or the immediate judgment scene.
Solomon's forces are gathered and ordered, providing a constructive contrast to Iblis's fully assembled forces.
A purported army cannot protect its adherents apart from the Merciful, directly illuminating the impotence of Iblis's troops.
Hell is declared to be filled with Iblis and all his followers, the closest parallel to their complete gathering in 26:95.
The people's admission of continual idol worship begins the local chain that culminates in false gods and Iblis's troops failing to help.
Lot and all his household are saved together, an opposed instance of a complete group receiving rescue rather than punishment.
All will be questioned, reinforcing the comprehensive accountability that frames Iblis's gathered followers.
The bare number does not materially clarify Iblis, troops, gathering, or the final judgment scene.
Lot and all his household are saved together, contrasting comprehensive rescue with comprehensive condemnation.
Iblis's nonparticipation in the angels' prostration directly identifies the rebellion from which his following proceeds.
The two groups meet in the Exodus confrontation, continuing the local imagery of opposing collectives and pursuit.
The promised end reveals which party has the weaker troop, linking apparent group strength to eventual judgment.
Iblis refuses to prostrate and voices his objection, directly supplying the character and motive behind his forces.
The question whether idols hear their callers directly advances the exposure of the powerless supports in the same passage.
All honor belongs to God, supplying a general theological contrast to any status or force claimed by Iblis's troops.
Pharaoh and his troops are seized and thrown into the sea together, a direct pattern of collective hostile force meeting collective ruin.
The righteous are gathered as an honored delegation, contrasting the destination and status of Iblis's gathered forces.

Iblis and his descendants are named as enemies, directly expanding the personal rebel into an enduring hostile following.
The question whether idols benefit or harm completes the local test of the alleged helpers that cannot save their adherents.
The Day of Decision gathers later and earlier people, furnishing the wider eschatological assembly for 26:95.
Hostile troops are met by unseen divine troops, contrasting visible military pressure with God's decisive support.
The appeal to ancestral practice explains the inherited idolatry being dismantled in the immediate context of 26:95.
The total subjection of creation concerns divine provision, not the formation or fate of Iblis's troops.
An overwhelming army is threatened as an instrument of judgment, showing military force under higher authority.
The verse distinguishes a limited counted guard from the wider forces known only to God, relativizing any apparent army.
Offering everyone on earth as ransom demonstrates that an amassed human total cannot purchase escape from punishment.
Pharaoh and his troops act arrogantly and deny return, connecting organized force with rebellion and final accountability.
Abraham calls attention to the objects of worship, directly continuing the local exposure of false allegiance.
The universal address concerns prophetic mission and does not specifically illuminate Iblis's troops or their judgment.
Pharaoh, Haman, and their troops are named as wrongdoers, linking a ruling force to moral culpability.
The inclusion of ancestral worshippers sharpens the inherited collective allegiance challenged in the surrounding argument.

Pharaoh and his troops are thrown into the sea together, a close example of a hostile force gathered into shared ruin.
Gathering and counting wealth concerns hoarding, not Iblis's followers or an army's final gathering.

Pharaoh, Haman, and their troops fear the reversal God will show them, joining military power to its threatened downfall.

Hell is filled with jinn and humans altogether, closely matching the complete eschatological gathering of Iblis's forces.

The contrast between guided and face-down walking does not materially clarify Iblis, troops, gathering, or judgment.

The forgiveness of all sins uses totality language but does not develop Iblis's troops or their final assembly.
Pharaoh and his troops pursue in transgression until drowning overtakes them, a close precedent for a hostile force's ruin.
The observation of birds in flight does not materially clarify Iblis, troops, gathering, or the final judgment scene.

Unseen divine troops support the Messenger, furnishing a contrast to the ultimately powerless troops of Iblis.
The immediate question asks whether the worshipped can help themselves or their followers, directly anticipating their failure.

Jinn and humans are gathered, their mutual allegiance is exposed, and the Fire is assigned, closely matching the judgment logic of 26:95.

God questions Iblis about his refusal, directly developing the rebellion whose followers are gathered in 26:95.
Iblis is expelled for arrogance, establishing the moral status of the leader of those troops.
Iblis asks for respite until resurrection, explicitly connecting his activity to the final day.
The granted respite enables the continuing work of the adversary whose followers later face judgment.
Iblis declares his plan to obstruct people from the straight path, directly explaining how his following is formed.
The attack from every direction describes the comprehensive strategy of Satanic misguidance behind the gathered host.
Hell is promised for Iblis and all who follow him, a direct parallel to the total assembly in 26:95.
On the Day of Judgment Satan disowns those who answered his call, directly exposing the failure of his gathered followers.
God addresses Iblis over his absence from the prostrators, directly continuing the origin of his rebellion.
Iblis rejects prostration to Adam on grounds of superiority, defining the arrogance behind his leadership.
Iblis is ordered out and declared expelled, establishing his separation from obedient ranks.
The curse upon Iblis until the Day of Recompense directly binds his rebellion to final judgment.
Iblis requests reprieve until resurrection, explicitly locating his activity within the eschatological horizon.
The granted reprieve explains the continued presence of Iblis before the final gathering.
The reprieve lasts to a known time, setting a fixed limit on Iblis's apparent freedom.
Iblis vows to make earthly life attractive and mislead people, directly explaining the recruitment of followers.
Iblis excludes God's sincere servants from his claim, distinguishing those outside his effective following.
God declares the straight path over which Iblis has no independent control.
Iblis has no authority over God's servants except those who follow him, directly defining his contingent host.
Iblis declares his intention to dominate Adam's descendants, directly expanding his prospective following.
Those who follow Iblis are warned that Hell is their full recompense.
Iblis is permitted to entice people and mobilize against them, using imagery of organized force and shared deception.
Iblis is denied authority over God's servants, sharply limiting the force attributed to his followers.
The dispute in Hell immediately continues the scene after Iblis's troops are gathered.
The condemned confess manifest error, supplying the judgment response of the assembled misguided.

They identify criminals as those who led them astray, clarifying the human agency within the misguiding collective.
The lack of intercessors immediately confirms that the assembled false supports cannot rescue anyone.
The absence of a devoted friend completes the scene of abandoned and powerless allegiance in Hell.
Iblis has no coercive authority; his following reveals who truly believes in the Hereafter, directly qualifying 34:20 and 26:95.
Satan is an enemy who calls his party to the Blaze, directly linking a satanic collective to Hell.

Iblis invokes his superiority over Adam, exposing the arrogance behind his rebellion.
Iblis is expelled from the divine presence, defining the separation of his camp from obedience.
The curse upon Iblis lasts until the Day of Recompense, tying him directly to final judgment.

Iblis swears to mislead all people through his might, directly describing the intended scope of his following.
The exception for God's sincere servants distinguishes those not captured by Iblis's misguidance.

Those overcome by Satan are called the party of Satan and declared losers, the closest collective counterpart to Iblis's troops.

Believers are told to fight the allies of Satan, explicitly presenting Satan as the center of an opposing collective.
False worship is joined to the worship of a rebellious Satan, directly linking idolatry with satanic allegiance.

Satan's promises to mislead, arouse desires, and command alteration explain the mechanisms by which his followers are formed.
Satan promises and arouses false hopes, directly exposing the deception behind allegiance to him.
Those followers have Hell as their refuge with no escape, matching the final destination of Iblis's troops.
Devils inspire their allies to dispute, showing a network of satanic influence rather than an isolated deceiver.
Satan whispers to Adam and his wife, an early instance of the deceptive method later attributed to his following.
Satan and his tribe are described as the agents who expelled Adam's parents and who see humans from concealment.

Satan makes deeds attractive and becomes the protector of those who reject, directly linking misguidance with allegiance.

Satan whispers to Adam, showing the concrete deceptive action of the enemy named Iblis in the same account.

Satan leads a person away from the reminder and then abandons him, directly paralleling the failure of false allies.
Satan makes a people’s sun worship appear attractive, directly joining false worship to satanic deception.
Satan beautifies past peoples' deeds and bars them from the path, a general pattern of collective misguidance.
Satan has already misled a great multitude, directly confirming the scale of his eventual gathered following.
Evil companions beautify what is before and behind their associates, showing organized reinforcement of misguidance.
Whoever turns from the Merciful receives a satanic companion, directly describing attachment to a deceiving ally.
Those companions turn people from the path while making them think they are guided, directly explaining false allegiance.
At judgment the deceived person wishes for distance from his satanic companion, exposing the ruin of that association.
The wrongdoing parties share punishment on that day, reinforcing the collective consequence of shared misguidance.
